tasks.q: Which of these are examples of people being a weak point? Select all that apply.
opts: Writing a password on a sticky note
Not logging off a shared computer
Leaving the server room door unlocked
Locking the screen when leaving a desk
correct: Writing a password on a sticky note
Not logging off a shared computer
Leaving the server room door unlocked
tasks.fb: The last two are good practice: they make people a strength instead.

tasks.q: Why do attackers target people rather than software?
a: People can be tricked, and it's often easier than defeating the technology
tasks.fb: Firewalls can't stop someone from holding a door open.

a: Inventing a convincing story to persuade someone to give information or access
Sending a fake email to thousands of people
Leaving an infected USB stick in a car park
tasks.fb: Blagging is done person to person, often by phone.

tasks.q: Someone phones claiming to be from IT and asks for your password to 'fix an error'. What should you do?
a: Refuse, and check with the IT team using a number you know
Give it, because IT staff can be trusted
Email it instead of saying it
tasks.fb: Genuine IT staff never need your password.

a: Watching someone enter their password or PIN to steal it
Carrying a server out of a building
tasks.fb: Cash machines and school logins are common targets.

tasks.q: How does tailgating get someone into a secure building?
a: They follow an authorised person through the door before it closes
They guess the door code with software
tasks.fb: Staff should politely challenge anyone without a pass.

a: Leaving something tempting, such as an infected USB stick, for a victim to use
tasks.fb: Curiosity is the weakness being exploited.

tasks.q: You find a USB stick in the car park labelled 'Staff salaries'. What should you do?
a: Hand it to the IT team without plugging it in
Plug it into a school computer to find the owner
Take it home and check it there
tasks.fb: Plugging it in is exactly what the attacker hopes for.

tasks.q: Match each technique to how it reaches the victim.
pairs: An infected USB stick or download
tasks.fb: They differ in the channel, but all are social engineering.

tasks.q: What is an acceptable use policy?
a: A document setting out the rules a user must agree to before using an organisation's network
tasks.fb: This is the definition from your lesson 9 matching task.

tasks.q: Which is the best defence against social engineering?
a: Training people to recognise the techniques, backed by clear policies
tasks.fb: Technology alone can't stop someone being persuaded.

tasks.q: Which technique does each incident describe?
items: A caller pretends to be the head teacher and asks for a password reset
Someone stands behind you while you type your PIN
A USB stick labelled 'Exam papers' is left in the corridor
An email claims your account will close unless you log in now
A stranger in a high-vis jacket says they're here to fix the servers
A free game download secretly installs malware
A camera is angled at the keypad by the office door
A text message asks you to confirm your bank details
tasks.fb: All four are social engineering: they target people, not technology.

info.title: The famous social engineer
info.text: Kevin Mitnick, once the FBI's most wanted hacker, said he got most of his access by simply asking people, rather than by breaking software.

info.title: USB drops work
info.text: In one study, researchers dropped USB sticks around a university car park. Around half were picked up and plugged into a computer.

info.title: Politeness is a weakness
info.text: Holding a door open is polite, but it also defeats an expensive door lock. Good security training tells staff it's fine to ask for a pass.

info.title: Caller ID lies
info.text: Phone numbers can be spoofed, so a call that appears to come from your bank may not. Hang up and call back on a number you know.

info.title: Screen privacy
info.text: Privacy filters make a screen look black from the side, which makes shouldering much harder in public places.

info.title: Clean desk
info.text: Many organisations have a clean-desk policy: no printouts or notes left out when you leave, so nothing sensitive is on show.
